paras.t: Because prayer is the raising of your heart and mind to
God, it is just as necessary for the life of your soul as
breathing is for the life of your body.
With the People of God you have to walk the same
road of Life. You praise, thank, and ask God for help.
At times you experience great joy in giving witness to
the life and teachings of Christ. Often, however,
spiritual, moral, and bodily miseries trouble your soul.
In such circumstances, St. Paul tells us, “When we
cannot choose words in order to pray properly, the
Spirit Himself asks for us; and God, who knows
everything in our hearts, knows perfectly well what
the Spirit desires.” (Rom.8 . 26-27).
In this prayer book are found the expressions of a deep
faith in a just and merciful God, who heals broken
hearts, binds up mens wounds, frees the oppressed,
feeds the hungry, sets captives free, give sight to the
blind, supports orphans and widows, pardons all
faults, above allCand in spite our inconsistencies— we
find a God who is faithful to his promises.
DAILY PSALMS AND CANTICLES is a book of hope, a
light to guide your way home. May your prayerful use
of it be for the greater glory of God and the salvation
of souls.
+ MICHAEL J. DEMPSEY, O.P.
15th August 1972
This book follows the arrangement of the Liturgy of the Hours, the official
prayer book of the Church. It contains a four week cycle of five daily prayers:
1) Morning, 2) Midday. 3) Evening, 4) Compline, and 5) Office of Readings,
which can be at any time. Of these the most important are Morning and
Evening Prayer.
Each hour begins with a call to prayer. For the first prayer of the day
(Morning or Office of Readings) it is Psalm 51:25, “Help me to speak, Lord.
And I will praise you.” This is followed by the Invitatory Psalm (See p.9). For
the other hours, the call to prayer is Psalm70:1, “Save me God. Lord help
me now.” This is followed by “Glory be to the Father... Amen. Halleluia.”

not that you follow each detail, but that you pray.

In this book the psalms are set out in strophes, or
paragraphs, each containing verses of 2 or 3 lines each. When the
Liturgy of the Hours is celebrated in common, two groups sing the
verses or strophes alternately. Some tones are meant for alternating
at each verse; others are for alternating after each strophe.
Strophic tones:
These tones are based on 4 lines fitting 2 verses. If the
strophe has only 1 verse the 1st and 4th lines are used, and the 2nd
if the verse has 3 lines. If the strophe has 3 verses, the last verse
repeats the 1st and 4th lines of the tone. When one of the verses
has 3 lines, the first line has a flex or is sung on a monotone followed
by a pause. The following are examples:
1. [mi] so/ [mi] fa/ [re] fa/ [re] do ti do
2. [mi] re do/ [do] re/ [fa] mi re/ [re] mi do
3. [mi] re do/ [do] ti la/ [so] la do/ [do] re do ti do
4. [so] fa mi/ [mi] re do/ [re] mi fa mi/ [re] do mi
5. [so] mi so/ [la] fa la/ [do] ti/ [la] so
6. [so] la do/ [do] mi re/ [do] la/ [la] so
7. [do] re mi/ [do] re mi fa mi/ [mi] re/ [re] mi re do
8. [do] ti/ [ti] la/[la] ti/ [ti] la so do
9. [so] la do/[do] mi re/ [do] la/ [la] re do
10. [so] do ti la/ [la] re do ti/ [ti] la/[la] ti do do so
11. [so] fa mi/ [so] do so la/[la] so fa/ [fa] so re mi
12. [la] do re mi/ [mi] fa re mi/ [mi] re do la/ [la] ti so la
13. [mi] re mi so/ [do] re mi/ [fa] mi re/ [re] do re
Tones alternating each verse:
1. [mi] re do/ [fa] mi re mi
2. [mi] re do/ [re] do la do
3. [mi] re do/ [do] re do re mi
4. [fa] so fa/ [fa] mi do re
5. do mi [so] la so/ [so] la fa..so mi

11. [do] re..do/ [do] fa mi fa
12. [mi] re mi fa/ [mi] do re ti // [do] la do re/ [do] la ti so

Note: For good community singing of the Psalms remember two
rhythmic rules: 1) Give one each syllable equal length. 2) Begin
immediately the other side finishes its verse or strophe, but after
each line of your own section pause for two beats.
